new_entities.name: Paced activity for long COVID
aliases: energy management pacing for long COVID
new_entities.description: An activity-management approach that aims to stay within an individual's exertional tolerance to reduce symptom flares in long COVID.

new_entities.name: Symptom burden
new_entities.description: The overall frequency, intensity, or functional burden of symptoms experienced by a patient.

edges.effect_quant: The most relevant review found that five rehabilitation studies involving 193 participants reported lower frequency or intensity of post-exertional malaise after tailored programmes centered on pacing approaches, but robust pooled treatment estimates were not available.
edges.population: adults with long COVID, especially those with fatigue or post-exertional symptom exacerbation
edges.mechanism: Pacing may reduce symptom burden by keeping activity below an individual's post-exertional trigger threshold and smoothing boom-bust cycles. At the same time, overt avoidance can reinforce deconditioning, and objective exercise-challenge work suggests not every long-COVID patient has reproducible post-exertional worsening, so pacing likely helps a subset more than the whole population.
edges.summary: The strongest anchor is the 2025 PEM review, which suggests that tailored rehabilitation programmes built around pacing can reduce PEM frequency or intensity in some long-COVID patients. But the evidence base is still thin, most of it is not direct head-to-head pacing research, and objective studies show a more heterogeneous exertional response than patient reports alone imply, so this edge should stay mixed and low-certainty.
edges.caveats: Direct randomized trials of pacing itself are still largely absent. Much of the available literature blends pacing with broader rehabilitation, self-management, or PEM screening, which makes it hard to distinguish a true pacing effect from careful patient selection or multimodal care.
